title: Bank of America’s ‘Robust’ AI Data Center Deal Pipeline: Q&A | BloombergNEF
gist: Bank of America's Karen Fang argues capital is no longer the binding constraint on AI data centers — power, chips, labor and interconnection are — and points to the Related Digital/Oracle Michigan project, where BofA replaced a stalling bank syndicate with a 19-year Pimco-anchored bond raising $14 billion of debt (the interviewer frames the facility as a $16 billion project), as the template for construction-through-operation project bonds. She rejects the AI-bubble framing on credit grounds (top four hyperscalers AA- or better, top three AI chip designers A- or better) while conceding the pace of capex — $700+ billion guided for 2026, ~75% above 2025 — is unprecedented.

insights.claim: Bank of America's global head of infrastructure and sustainable finance says capital availability is not the limiting factor for AI data center buildout; the binding constraints are power infrastructure, skilled labor, equipment and supply chains.
insights.speaker: Karen Fang
insights.so_what: If financing is not the throttle, credit-spread widening won't slow the buildout — watch turbine, transformer, HBM and electrician bottlenecks instead as the real cycle governors.
insights.quote: The primary constraints are now real-world execution challenges. While capital remains abundant, the pace of growth will be determined by the availability of power infrastructure, skilled labor, equipment and supply chains.
insights.locator: Q: At the BNEF Summit in New York recently you said money wasn’t the main constraint

insights.claim: Data center projects are increasingly funded from Treasury, municipal, investment-grade and high-yield credit pools rather than traditional bank construction loans, broadening the capital base as the asset class matures.
insights.speaker: Karen Fang
insights.so_what: Bank balance-sheet capacity is no longer the ceiling on deal size; watch for data center paper becoming a growing share of IG index issuance.
insights.quote: Trillions of dollars are already deployed across US Treasuries, municipal bonds, and investment-grade and high-yield credit markets.
insights.locator: A: Capital availability is not the limiting factor.

insights.claim: Bank of America's view is that data centers are not yet being overbuilt because only a limited portion of announced projects ever reach construction, filtered by power availability, memory and chip supply, labor shortages, interconnection capacity, cooling, water and community consent.
insights.speaker: Karen Fang
insights.so_what: Announced-pipeline gigawatt figures materially overstate real demand for power, land and chips — discount headline announcement trackers when sizing supplier order books.
insights.quote: Industry data indicates that only a limited portion of announced projects advance to the construction stage, underscoring the practical challenges of delivering large-scale infrastructure at speed.
insights.locator: Q: So, data center building isn’t outstripping demand right now?

insights.claim: A persistent gap between data center demand and deliverable supply is framed by Bank of America as a capital-allocation opportunity rather than a market failure, justifying selectivity toward projects that can actually be delivered.
insights.speaker: Karen Fang
insights.so_what: Expect lender bifurcation: tier-one sponsors get bond-market pricing while marginal developers are starved, so credit dispersion inside the sector should widen.
insights.quote: Rather than viewing the supply-demand gap as a negative, it should be recognized as an opportunity to prioritize high-quality projects, allocate capital more efficiently
insights.locator: Rather than viewing the supply-demand gap

themes.theme: Michigan/Oracle deal: the 19-year project bond template

insights.claim: Bank of America structured a 19-year term financing with callability starting in year three for the Michigan data center leased to Oracle, replacing the conventional three-year construction loan plus post-completion refinancing with permanent debt raised from the outset.
insights.speaker: Karen Fang
insights.so_what: A replicable structure that moves multi-billion data center construction risk from bank balance sheets to long-duration bond investors — watch for copycat project bonds in 2026-27 issuance calendars.
insights.quote: The result was an innovative 19-year term financing structure with callability starting in year three.
insights.locator: Q: Bank of America was a structuring agent and financial advisor for the $16 billion Michigan facility

insights.claim: The Michigan data center financing pivoted to the bond market in early January after some banks in the assembled syndicate balked at the size of the $14 billion debt raise, with Pimco taking the lead in the bond discussions.
insights.speaker: Karen Fang
insights.so_what: Bank syndicate capacity is already binding at the $10bn+ single-project level — the marginal buyer of AI infrastructure risk is now a bond fund, not a lending desk.
insights.quote: We assembled a bank syndicate, but given the significant size of the financing, some lenders expressed concerns about capacity.
insights.locator: The key question for the Michigan transaction

insights.claim: Related Digital secured Oracle as anchor tenant at its Michigan site and worked with utility DTE to tap existing excess grid power, so the project needed only incremental battery storage and substation connectivity rather than new generation.
insights.speaker: Karen Fang
insights.so_what: Sites with stranded utility headroom are the scarce asset in data center underwriting — screen developers and utilities by spare interconnected capacity, not land bank.
insights.quote: That was a huge differentiator because it meant no new generation was required, only incremental battery storage and substation connectivity was needed.
insights.locator: This deal originated last July, and we executed in April

insights.claim: The Michigan bond offered investors an attractive risk premium relative to standard hyperscaler credit instruments while leaving the sponsors free to refinance from year three.
insights.speaker: Karen Fang
insights.so_what: Project-level data center bonds price wide of hyperscaler corporate paper on essentially the same tenant credit — a spread pickup credit investors can harvest.
insights.quote: The fixed coupon investment provided investors with an attractive risk premium relative to the standard hyperscaler credit instruments while preserving the sponsors’ flexibility to refinance should that become feasible.
insights.locator: The result was an innovative 19-year term financing structure

insights.claim: The Michigan transaction took roughly nine months from origination last July to execution in April, indicating the realistic clock for structuring a first-of-kind gigawatt-scale data center bond.
insights.speaker: Karen Fang
insights.so_what: A nine-month financing lead time is a hard floor on how fast announced AI capex can convert into steel and megawatts.
insights.quote: This deal originated last July, and we executed in April, so it was roughly a nine-month process.
insights.locator: A: This deal originated last July

insights.claim: Bank of America expects the success of the Michigan structure to push more data center projects into the long-term bond market to fund both construction and operation.
insights.speaker: Karen Fang
insights.so_what: Anticipate a new supply channel of long-dated data center project bonds competing with utility and REIT paper for insurance and pension duration demand.
insights.quote: We believe with the success of the Michigan data center financing, more projects will tap long-term debt in the bond market to cover construction and operation of such assets.
insights.locator: We believe with the success of the Michigan data center financing

insights.claim: Bank of America retains only limited residual exposure to the Michigan project via the debt interest reserve after its bridge loan was fully repaid, illustrating the originate-to-distribute posture banks are taking on AI infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Karen Fang
insights.so_what: Bank equity holders' AI data center risk may be far smaller than headline arranged volumes suggest; fee income, not credit exposure, is the earnings channel.
insights.quote: We extended a bridge loan, which has since been fully repaid. We retain limited exposure related to the debt interest reserve, which is typical for banks involved in the structuring.
insights.locator: Q: You have some exposure to the Michigan project too

themes.theme: Capex trajectory and the shift toward chip financing

insights.claim: The top four US hyperscalers have guided to more than $700 billion of capex for 2026, roughly 75% above 2025, with estimates still being revised upward each quarter.
insights.speaker: Karen Fang
insights.so_what: A ~75% year-on-year step-up sets the revenue base case for accelerator, power equipment and construction supply chains — and the level whose deceleration would mark the cycle turn.
insights.quote: The top four US hyperscalers have guided capex to $700+ billion for 2026 which is an approximately 75% increase from 2025 and estimates continue to revise upward with each quarter.
insights.locator: Q: What sort of growth are you seeing for data centers seeking financing?

insights.claim: BofA Research estimates the total addressable market for AI accelerators (GPUs and AI-specific ASICs) reaches $1.1 trillion in 2030, up from $200 billion of sales in 2025 and an estimated $380 billion this year.
insights.speaker: Karen Fang
insights.so_what: Implies roughly 90% growth in accelerator sales in 2026 alone and a ~24% CAGR thereafter to 2030 — a yardstick against which to test semiconductor consensus estimates.
insights.quote: the total addressable market for AI accelerators (GPUs and AI specific ASICs, or Application-Specific Integrated Circuits) will be $1.1 trillion in 2030 from $200 billion of sales in 2025 and an estimated $380 billion sales this year
insights.locator: For chips, BofA Research estimates

insights.claim: Inbound financing interest for chips and equipment now exceeds interest in data center shell financings at Bank of America, and chip-deployment financing demand has increased significantly of late.
insights.speaker: Karen Fang
insights.so_what: A leading indicator that GPU-backed lending, equipment leasing and securitization — not real estate — is the fastest-growing credit exposure in the AI complex.
insights.quote: Activity levels have increased materially, with inbound interest on chips and equipment financing exceeding data center shell financings.
insights.locator: Q: What sort of growth are you seeing for data centers seeking financing?

insights.claim: Beyond balance-sheet construction loans, Bank of America is increasingly using project bonds, equipment and inventory leasing structures, and securitized products to finance the AI infrastructure ecosystem.
insights.speaker: Karen Fang
insights.so_what: Securitized GPU and equipment paper is an emerging asset class — and a place where AI credit risk migrates out of visible bank disclosures.
insights.quote: we are increasingly utilizing project bonds, equipment and inventory leasing structures, and securitized products to respond to the scale and evolving needs of this ecosystem
insights.locator: Q: What other key data center or related projects has BofA been involved in?

insights.claim: Data center financing differs from plain-vanilla infrastructure in requiring simultaneous competence across three distinct financing categories — energy and power, the data center shell, and chips plus equipment — with material tax and accounting considerations.
insights.speaker: Karen Fang
insights.so_what: A three-pillar lens for evaluating which arrangers and developers can actually clear large AI projects; single-discipline players get disintermediated.
insights.quote: The financing is often done across the three categories – energy and power, the data center shell, and the chips plus equipment – so we need to be proficient in all three.
insights.locator: Q: How is structuring and advising financing for a data center different from plain vanilla infrastructure?

themes.theme: Bubble rebuttal grounded in credit quality

insights.claim: The AI buildout differs from the dot-com bubble because the entities funding the capex are exceptionally strong credits: the top four hyperscalers are rated AA- or above and the three largest AI-focused chip designers A- or above, with significant operating cash flows even after capex increases.
insights.speaker: Karen Fang
insights.so_what: The bull case rests on funding coming from cash flow and AA balance sheets rather than leverage — so a downgrade or a shift to debt-funded capex at a top-four hyperscaler is the signal that the analogy breaks.
insights.quote: The top four hyperscalers are all AA- credits and above and the three largest AI focused chip designers are rated A- and above as well
insights.locator: Q: What do you say to those people who say AI is a bubble?

insights.claim: Even while rejecting the bubble label, Bank of America concedes the pace and scale of AI infrastructure investment is unprecedented and that the technology cycle will produce clear winners and losers, justifying selective underwriting.
insights.speaker: Karen Fang
insights.so_what: The lender's own hedge: expect tightening credit selectivity at the project level well before any macro turn in AI sentiment.
insights.quote: As with any transformative technology cycle, there will be winners and losers.
insights.locator: From an infrastructure and financing perspective, however

insights.claim: Bank of America is managing AI infrastructure growth through capital recycling and velocity rather than balance-sheet accumulation, preserving capacity for future deals while staying within risk appetite.
insights.speaker: Karen Fang
insights.so_what: Bank AI exposure should be judged on distribution capability, not commitments — if bond and securitization bids soften, arranged volumes stall quickly.
insights.quote: we remain disciplined in our approach – focused on capital recycling and velocity and managing exposures within our risk appetite while preserving significant capacity to support future growth
insights.locator: Our commitments have grown alongside that demand

insights.claim: Hyperscaler and AI customers are underwriting projects on certainty of delivery, execution capability, minimized construction risk, permitting readiness and reliable power access — the same criteria the lender uses.
insights.speaker: Karen Fang
insights.so_what: A five-point screen for which data center developers win contracts; permitting and power access are the discriminators, not cost of capital.
insights.quote: hyperscalers and AI customers are focused on the same fundamentals as we are: certainty of delivery, strong execution capabilities, minimizing construction risk, permitting readiness and reliable access to power
insights.locator: We positioned to be selective

themes.theme: Grid strain, community backlash and regulation

insights.claim: Global data center compute power draw crossed 60 gigawatts at end-2025 after adding over 12 gigawatts during the year, and US data center power use is projected to more than double by 2030 to 118 gigawatts in BNEF's base case.
insights.speaker: Vandana Gombar
insights.so_what: Anchors the load-growth thesis for US utilities, gas turbines and grid equipment; 118GW by 2030 is the number to test against interconnection queues.
insights.quote: The total power drawn by compute equipment at data centers globally crossed 60 gigawatts at the end of 2025, with over 12 gigawatts of demand added over the year, according to the latest BNEF update.
insights.locator: Data center additions have soared since the advent of ChatGPT

insights.claim: Political backlash over rising consumer power bills has begun producing hard supply constraints, with New York announcing a one-year moratorium on hyperscale data center facilities.
insights.speaker: Vandana Gombar
insights.so_what: Siting risk is now a state-level political variable — moratoria concentrate demand into permissive jurisdictions and raise the value of already-permitted sites.
insights.quote: The most recent pushback against data centers came from the state of New York, which announced a one-year moratorium on hyperscale facilities.
insights.locator: Power grids are struggling as a result

insights.claim: Data centers are 30-plus-year assets, so today's siting, design and energy choices lock in costs, reliability and community acceptance for decades — the argument for front-loading efficiency and community engagement over speed.
insights.speaker: Karen Fang
insights.so_what: Long asset lives mean stranded-asset risk if efficiency standards tighten mid-life; favors developers designing above current code.
insights.quote: These facilities are long-lived infrastructure assets, often operating for more than 30 years, meaning today’s siting, design, and energy choices will shape costs, reliability, and stakeholder perceptions for decades.
insights.locator: Q: Singapore now requires data centers to be more power efficient than the global average

insights.claim: Bank of America expects the US to continue favoring incentive-based, market-driven data center policy while other jurisdictions such as Singapore lean on efficiency mandates.
insights.speaker: Karen Fang
insights.so_what: Regulatory arbitrage favors US siting economics near-term, but concentrates the political-backlash risk domestically.
insights.quote: Some jurisdictions may lean more heavily on regulatory approaches, while the US has historically favored incentive-based, market-driven policies to encourage investment and innovation.
insights.locator: Q: Singapore now requires data centers to be more power efficient

themes.theme: Efficiency, flexible load and the clean-power tailwind

insights.claim: AI workloads can be dispatched as flexible load — shifting training tasks to regions with surplus renewable generation and scaling back where power is constrained — turning data centers into a tool for reducing renewable curtailment.
insights.speaker: Karen Fang
insights.so_what: Geographic load-shifting is the lender's answer to grid strain; watch whether hyperscaler contracts actually price this flexibility, which would change renewable curtailment economics.
insights.quote: AI training tasks can be shifted to regions experiencing surplus renewable generation and scaled back in areas facing power constraints.
insights.locator: From a sustainable infrastructure financing perspective

insights.claim: Capital allocation in AI infrastructure will increasingly favor platforms and technologies delivering higher computational output per unit of energy, making compute-per-watt a determinant of long-term asset competitiveness.
insights.speaker: Karen Fang
insights.so_what: Efficiency gains cut both ways for power demand forecasts — improving compute-per-watt could reduce the need for new generation capacity that utility bulls are pricing in.
insights.quote: Over time, improved efficiency could reduce the need for additional power generation capacity, lower operating costs, and help address community concerns about the energy footprint of large-scale data center projects.
insights.locator: At the same time, rapid advances in chip design

insights.claim: AI and digital infrastructure growth is acting as a tailwind for renewables and storage as well as newer baseload options including advanced geothermal, nuclear and small modular reactors, within Bank of America's $924 billion of sustainable finance mobilized from 2021 to 2025 against a $1.5 trillion ten-year goal.
insights.speaker: Karen Fang
insights.so_what: Confirms bank capital is flowing to SMR and geothermal on the back of AI load growth — a funding channel to track for pre-revenue baseload developers.
insights.quote: The growth of AI and digital infrastructure has provided tailwinds for renewable energy and storage projects, as well as newer forms of baseload power such as advanced geothermal and nuclear and SMR [Small Modular Reactors]technologies.
insights.locator: Q: Are you still tracking your sustainable financing target?

insights.claim: Bank of America says it has enabled construction of over 5 gigawatts of data center projects globally in the last 18 months and set up a Global Capital Solutions business last fall to act as a single coordination point for hyperscalers and developers.
insights.speaker: Karen Fang
insights.so_what: Signals banks are reorganizing internally around AI infrastructure as a distinct vertical — a fee pool worth tracking in capital markets revenue lines.
insights.quote: BofA says it has enabled the construction of over 5 gigawatts of data center projects globally over the last 18 months.
insights.locator: BofA says it has enabled the construction of over 5 gigawatts

insights.claim: Equity investors in large-scale data center developments should expect capital recovery over roughly five to 15 years, with wide variance driven by financing costs and lease terms.
insights.speaker: Karen Fang
insights.so_what: A 5-15 year payback band is long relative to 3-5 year GPU depreciation cycles — the duration mismatch is where data center equity risk actually sits.
insights.quote: equity investors in large-scale infrastructure and data center developments may expect capital recovery over a period ranging from approximately five to 15 years
insights.locator: Q: What can you tell us about payback periods on data center financing?
